@graph.name: Parathyroid Hormone (Intact PTH) Test
@graph.description: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) regulates calcium, phosphate and bone–kidney physiology. The meaning of a PTH result depends first on simultaneous calcium and kidney function; an in-range PTH can be inappropriate when calcium is high. PTH alone cannot determine whether hyperparathyroidism is primary, secondary or tertiary.

mainEntity.name: What is an intact PTH test?

acceptedAnswer.text: A blood immunoassay measuring parathyroid hormone to evaluate calcium, phosphate and bone-mineral physiology.

mainEntity.name: Why should PTH be tested with calcium?

acceptedAnswer.text: Calcium tells the clinician whether the PTH response is appropriate; a stand-alone PTH value is often misleading.

mainEntity.name: Can PTH be normal when calcium is high?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A laboratory-normal PTH may be inappropriately unsuppressed in hypercalcaemia and can indicate a PTH-dependent process.

mainEntity.name: What does high PTH with normal calcium mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: Possible secondary hyperparathyroidism from low vitamin D, CKD or malabsorption; normocalcaemic primary hyperparathyroidism is a diagnosis of exclusion.

mainEntity.name: What does high PTH with low calcium mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is usually an appropriate response to low calcium and may suggest vitamin D deficiency, CKD or malabsorption.

mainEntity.name: What does low PTH with high calcium mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: It suggests a PTH-independent cause and needs clinical work-up for malignancy, vitamin D-related or other disorders.

mainEntity.name: Can vitamin D deficiency raise PTH?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Reduced calcium absorption can stimulate secondary PTH secretion.

mainEntity.name: Does kidney disease increase PTH?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often. CKD may alter phosphate balance and active vitamin D synthesis, producing secondary hyperparathyroidism.

mainEntity.name: Can a kidney stone be caused by high PTH?

acceptedAnswer.text: Primary hyperparathyroidism can contribute to calcium stones, but not all stones are due to parathyroid disease.

mainEntity.name: Does high PTH mean a parathyroid tumour?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is common; biochemical classification comes first.

mainEntity.name: Is parathyroid disease the same as thyroid disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Parathyroid glands regulate calcium; the thyroid primarily regulates metabolic hormones.

mainEntity.name: What is primary hyperparathyroidism?

acceptedAnswer.text: A condition of autonomous PTH secretion, commonly with high calcium and non-suppressed PTH, confirmed biochemically.

mainEntity.name: What is secondary hyperparathyroidism?

acceptedAnswer.text: Compensatory PTH elevation due to disturbances such as low vitamin D, CKD or malabsorption.

mainEntity.name: What is tertiary hyperparathyroidism?

acceptedAnswer.text: Autonomous PTH excess after longstanding secondary hyperparathyroidism, generally in advanced renal disease.

mainEntity.name: Can calcium be normal in primary hyperparathyroidism?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes in carefully defined normocalcaemic PHPT, but only after repeated testing and exclusion of secondary causes.

mainEntity.name: Is an ultrasound needed to diagnose primary hyperparathyroidism?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The biochemical diagnosis precedes localisation imaging for surgery planning.

mainEntity.name: Why do doctors ask for vitamin D and phosphate with PTH?

acceptedAnswer.text: These values help distinguish primary from secondary physiology and identify mineral-bone disturbances.

mainEntity.name: What is ionised calcium?

acceptedAnswer.text: The biologically active unbound calcium fraction; it may be useful when total calcium is confounded by albumin or acid–base changes.

mainEntity.name: Can albumin affect total calcium?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Total calcium reflects protein-bound calcium; low albumin can lower total calcium without equivalent reduction in ionised calcium.

mainEntity.name: Does high PTH cause osteoporosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Persistently excessive PTH may affect skeletal health, but fracture risk depends on the underlying condition and other factors.

mainEntity.name: Can dehydration cause high calcium?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dehydration can concentrate some blood analytes and worsen hypercalcaemia; severe symptoms require urgent assessment.

mainEntity.name: What is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia?

acceptedAnswer.text: An inherited condition with mild high calcium and usually low urine calcium; it can resemble primary hyperparathyroidism.

mainEntity.name: Can medicines affect PTH and calcium?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lithium, thiazides, vitamin D, calcium supplements and antiresorptive medicines may alter interpretation.

mainEntity.name: Is fasting necessary for PTH?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not universally. Confirm QXL sample instructions; consistent timing can be useful for serial assessment.

mainEntity.name: Does PTH change during the day?

acceptedAnswer.text: PTH has biological variation and diurnal patterns; consistent collection conditions improve trends.

mainEntity.name: Should PTH be repeated?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, especially when confirming PHPT or reviewing CKD-MBD; clinical interpretation relies on trends.

mainEntity.name: Can a blood sample delay alter PTH?

acceptedAnswer.text: Potentially. Appropriate specimen type, separation and temperature control are method-dependent and important.

mainEntity.name: Can I diagnose vitamin D deficiency from PTH alone?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Measure 25-OH vitamin D directly and interpret alongside calcium and kidney function.

mainEntity.name: Does PTH always need surgery when high?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Management depends on the cause, severity, symptoms and established criteria.

mainEntity.name: When is low calcium an emergency?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tetany, seizures, spasms of the airway, fainting or heart-rhythm symptoms require urgent evaluation.
